query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid‐solution state are governed by the alloy’s inherent inability to impede dislocation glide. That is, the high symmetry and chemical disorder in the solid solution produce a low lattice friction and a lack of significant short-range ordering or precipitate formation, which precludes conventional obstacles to dislocation motion and consequently limits work‐hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi processed to form a chemically disordered, single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal treatment (aging/annealing) intended to promote nanoscale Ti-rich precipitate or ordering formation, which would serve as dislocation barriers.
generation.conditions: Samples should be deformed under quasi-static loading (tensile or compressive tests) at room temperature, keeping strain rate and environmental conditions identical between the as-cast solid-solution state and the precipitate-strengthened variant.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence (or absence) of nanoscale precipitates or short-range order acting as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: In the as-cast solid solution, the dislocation glide faces little resistance due to the absence of secondary phases and limited local lattice distortions (beyond average randomness), which results in lower resistance (hardness and strength). In contrast, thermally-induced nano-precipitates or ordering would create barriers that impede dislocation motion, thereby strengthening the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation testing, the thermally treated (aged) alloy variant is expected to show significantly increased hardness and yield strength compared to the as-cast simple solid solution, though possibly at the cost of some ductility. The as-cast alloy will demonstrate homogeneous dislocation glide with minimal work hardening.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties of the as-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi that exhibits favorable plasticity and machinability but lower hardness and strength.
generation.boundary: Applicable to compositions near equimolar Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti processed to a single-phase solid solution and tested under quasi-static room-temperature loading conditions. The hypothesis is relevant as long as no extrinsic precipitate-forming elements or severe nonequilibrium processing introduce additional strengthening mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While the model based on dislocation mobility is consistent with observed low hardness in simple solid solutions, the exact contribution of possible short-range chemical ordering and any subtle local lattice distortions remains to be fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples. Keep one set in the as-cast solid-solution state and subject the second set to a controlled aging treatment designed to promote the formation of nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates or ordering. Conduct identical quasi-static tensile or compression tests, complemented by in situ microscopy (e.g., TEM) to observe dislocation behavior.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging of dislocation motion
Phase/precipitate analysis using XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not display a significant increase in hardness and yield strength (or reveal no substantial change in dislocation interactions) compared to the as-cast solid-solution samples under identical testing conditions, the proposed hypothesis that facile dislocation glide (due to absence of barriers) governs low hardness and strength would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
